To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a new TPG for BIST that can reduce switching activity is proposed, which consists of two LFSRs, and is called the dual-speed LFSRs.
the use of DS-LSFs in the BIST of sequential circuits can reduce switching activity by up to 70% without any loss of fault coverage.

a test pattern generator (DS-LFSRs) is proposed that reduces switching activity during test generation, and the proposed DS-LFSRs reduce the number of load-capacitated weighted transitions by 13% to70% without loss of fault coverage and with slight area overheads.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a BIST TPC for low switching activity, and a procedure for designing such a TPG for any given combinational circuit.
the design and evaluation of a TPG for BIST that can reduce switching activity.
the design of a test pattern generator (DS-LFSRs) for built-in-self test (BIST), that can reduce switching activity at the circuit inputs during test application.

the proposed technique is very useful in reducing switching activity during test, and hence, in reducing the test power.
the proposed DS-LFSR can be used for low switching activity during test generation and test application.
the DS-LFSR is an effective TPG for low power BIST, with the ability to reduce switching activity during the application of tests.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed TPG can be used in BIST applications to reduce switching activity during the testing of combinational circuits.
the proposed TPG, DS-LFSR, is a very promising alternative to the conventional LFSR for BIST.
the DS-LFSR can be a very effective TPG for BIST.

a TPG can be designed to achieve high fault coverages with a low switching activity during test.
, in addition to reducing switching activity, DS-LFSR can also reduce the number of load-capacitive weighted transitions, thereby reducing the test power.

, for the ISCAS benchmark circuits, the number of transitions at the primary inputs is reduced by at least a factor of 1.4, with no loss of stuck-at or transition delay fault coverage, and with very small increase in the area overhead.
